prize_parts.citation: For establishing liquid-liquid phase separation of multivalent biomolecules as a physical-chemical principle organizing cells without membranes

statement.case_for: Biomolecular condensates supply a new concept of molecular organisation: phase behaviour, multivalency and interfacial thermodynamics explain how cytoplasm and nucleus are compartmentalised without membranes. The idea is physical chemistry in the strict sense, it is quantitative (saturation concentrations, thresholds, valency), and it has been confirmed in many systems by many independent groups. It has changed how cell biology, neurodegeneration research (including the amyloid link I work on) and even drug discovery frame their questions. It also gives the committee a prize that is clearly chemistry about the chemistry of life rather than synthesis or a method, and the Hyman/Brangwynne 2009 P-granule work plus Rosen's multivalency framework give a credible three-person core.
statement.case_against: The attribution cannot be cleanly bounded at three: Pappu and Mittag's sequence-grammar and theory work and Rosen's biochemistry make the cut contestable, and a committee could judge that the discovery belongs to cell biology and so to Medicine. There is also real, unresolved debate over which in vivo assemblies are equilibrium phase-separated liquids versus other assemblies, and over functional versus incidental condensation. A skeptic can argue the concept is still being tested and that a citation should wait for firmer mechanistic evidence.

responses.point: Heiner ranks base editing first and places condensates third, arguing that the physiological relevance and material state of many reported condensates are still debated and that a clean citation may be somewhat early.
responses.response: I accept that the in vivo debate is real, and I would not credit every reported condensate. But the principle itself, that multivalent macromolecules demix above a threshold concentration and that this organises cellular space, has been shown with purified components in vitro and in cells, and the citation can be limited to that principle. Maturity is a question of the concept, not of each application. I also note that base editing is a strong chemical-biology tool, but its long-term clinical record is only beginning, so I do not see it as the more mature of the two. I take his point about a clear three-person cut and agree that Pappu and Mittag are the strongest reason for caution.

responses.point: Johan ranks Car-Parrinello molecular dynamics first, arguing that a two-person, unambiguous 1985 priority and four decades of use make recognition overdue, and he places degraders second.
responses.response: I ranked Car and Parrinello fifth, and I agree on attribution and maturity: this is the cleanest credit on the list and the method is everywhere in condensed-phase chemistry. My reservation is on breadth of the concept rather than on quality. Its influence is enabling and computational, whereas I would weigh a discovery that introduced a new physical picture of how matter is organised in living cells slightly higher. I would not oppose it as a prize, and I would like to hear how he weighs a computational-method prize against a conceptual one this year.

responses.point: Daniel ranks targeted protein degradation first, arguing that hijacking E3 ligases with rational heterobifunctional molecules or glues is a new pharmacological principle and that the field is broadly reproduced and clinically advancing.
responses.response: I put B052 low, seventh, and I want to say why fairly: the principle is genuinely new and chemically clever, but the attribution is the most fragmented on the list (Crews, Deshaies, Handa, Ciulli, Gray, Sakamoto, Kim, Ito), the three-person cut leaves out several people with major claims, and Daniel himself concedes approval of a PROTAC drug is still pending. I would ask whether that is the right moment, compared with condensates, where the concept is established across fields. I do not dismiss it, and I recognise it is the strongest first-place case among the medicinal chemistry candidates.

responses.point: Andrei ranks sequencing-by-synthesis first, stressing that the reversible-terminator chemistry is a well-defined, universally adopted reaction scheme that is exceptionally mature and arguably overdue, with a clean two-person credit.
responses.response: I agree that it is mature and chemically concrete, and the Balasubramanian and Klenerman credit is cleaner than for many candidates. My concern is that the platform story is entangled with 454, clustered amplification and commercial development, and the prize would be read as honouring an instrument and a technology rather than a new chemical principle. I would want the committee to be sure the citation could be limited to the reversible-terminator chemistry before I support it over a conceptual advance.

uncertainties: Whether the committee would treat liquid-liquid phase separation in cells as chemistry rather than cell biology, and whether Pappu and Mittag can be left out defensibly.
Whether the unresolved in vivo debate about which condensates are genuine phase-separated liquids is serious enough to make B063 premature.
How much the 2023 Medicine prize for nucleoside modification and the 2024 Chemistry prize on protein structure prediction should discount B062 and B036 respectively.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for any shortlisted candidate. I note only that I share a field with the condensate and lipid-nanoparticle candidates (soft matter, lipid self-assembly) and that Heiner Linke and Peter Somfai are Lund colleagues, which is not a recusal matter.
